item.title: The Sleeping Gypsy
item.museum: The Museum of Modern Art, New York
item.lesson: Henri Rousseau was a Paris toll collector — 'Le Douanier,' the customs man, his friends teased — who taught himself to paint and believed, with unshakable sincerity, that he was the equal of the academic masters he admired. The academy laughed; the avant-garde eventually understood. Under a full moon, a lion pauses over a sleeping traveler with her mandolin and water jar, sniffing but not striking. A desert of pure stage-set flatness rolls to distant mountains; every fold and star is rendered with the meticulousness of a man who never learned what to leave out — which is precisely the magic. The scene obeys dream logic: nothing explains it, and nothing needs to. Rousseau offered it to his hometown for a modest price; they declined. He died poor in 1910, two years after Picasso threw a half-mocking, half-worshipful banquet in his honor. The Surrealists later canonized him: painting's great inventor of the dream you cannot interpret, only enter.
item.lookFor: Check the lion's eye — a bright, worried sideways glance, as if it, too, is unsure it belongs in this dream. And note the woman's open eye-slit: she may not be asleep at all.
